evidence: prob.txt

Data: customer records with
labels: churned / stayed.
Goal: predict churn for
new customers.
scenarios.hint: Labeled examples predicting a label — which paradigm?
scenarios.situation: Customer records labeled churned/stayed must predict churn for new customers.
scenarios.title: Learning from labeled history
scenarios.why: Supervised learning trains on labeled examples to predict labels for new data — exactly the churn problem. Unsupervised finds structure without labels; reinforcement learns from rewards; deep learning is an implementation approach, not the paradigm here.

evidence: fraud2.txt

Fraud: 0.1% of transactions.
Missing fraud costs $500 each.
False alarms cost $0.50 review.
scenarios.hint: Missing positives is 1000x costlier than false alarms — which error matters?
scenarios.prompt: Which metric should guide model selection?
scenarios.situation: Fraud is 0.1% of transactions; missing fraud costs $500, false alarms cost $0.50.
scenarios.title: The $500 miss vs the $0.50 alarm
scenarios.why: Recall (catching actual fraud) dominates because misses cost 1000x false alarms — but F1 balances both so precision doesn't collapse entirely. Accuracy is meaningless at 0.1% prevalence (99.9% by guessing 'not fraud'); precision alone would miss fraud.

choices: Overfitting — regularize, get more data, or simplify
Data leakage — remove the test set
evidence: fit.txt

Train accuracy: 99%.
Validation accuracy: 61%.
Gap widening with epochs.
scenarios.hint: Huge train/validation gap — what is the model doing?
scenarios.prompt: What is happening and what fixes it?
scenarios.situation: Training accuracy is 99% but validation is 61%, with the gap widening.
scenarios.title: 99% on training, 61% on reality
scenarios.why: The classic overfitting signature: the model memorizes training data instead of generalizing. Fixes: regularization, more/diverse data, simpler model, early stopping. Underfitting shows low training accuracy too; the test set isn't the problem; shipping a 38-point gap is not an option.

evidence: split.txt

Data: 100k labeled rows.
Need: train, tune hyperparameters,
and get an unbiased final estimate.
scenarios.hint: Which split must stay untouched until the very end?
scenarios.prompt: Which split gives the unbiased final estimate?
scenarios.situation: 100k labeled rows must support training, hyperparameter tuning, and an unbiased final estimate.
scenarios.title: Three splits, three jobs
scenarios.why: The test set stays locked until final evaluation, giving the unbiased estimate; validation tunes hyperparameters; training fits parameters. Tuning on the test set leaks it; training on everything leaves no honest estimate.

evidence: reg.txt

Goal: predict house prices
(a continuous value) from
features like size and location.
scenarios.hint: Continuous target value — which task type?
scenarios.situation: Predicting house prices (a continuous value) from features like size and location.
scenarios.title: Predicting a number, not a label
scenarios.why: Regression predicts continuous values like prices. Classification predicts discrete labels; clustering groups unlabeled data; anomaly detection finds outliers — none fit a continuous price target.

choices: More training data always fixes it
The model is biased — audit features, rebalance, and add fairness metrics
Remove all demographic features and declare victory
evidence: bias.txt

Loan model: 92% accuracy overall,
but 40% false-rejection rate for
one demographic group.
scenarios.hint: High overall accuracy hiding group harm — what must be measured?
scenarios.situation: A loan model shows 92% overall accuracy but a 40% false-rejection rate for one demographic group.
scenarios.title: 92% accurate, still unfair
scenarios.why: Aggregate accuracy hides group-level harm; the response is auditing features/labels for bias, rebalancing data, and tracking fairness metrics (e.g., equalized odds) alongside accuracy. More data alone doesn't fix biased labels; removing demographic features doesn't remove proxies; accuracy-only thinking caused this.

evidence: sm.txt

Team: 5 data scientists.
Need: shared notebooks, managed
training, experiment tracking.
scenarios.hint: Which AWS service is the managed ML platform?
scenarios.situation: Five data scientists need shared notebooks, managed training, and experiment tracking.
scenarios.title: The ML platform, managed
scenarios.why: SageMaker provides Studio notebooks, managed training jobs, and experiment tracking as one platform. Manual EC2/laptop/bare-metal setups reintroduce ops and don't scale collaboration.

evidence: feat.txt

Features computed 3 ways by
3 teams; training/serving skew
causing bad predictions.
scenarios.hint: Which service is the central feature repository for training and serving?
scenarios.situation: Three teams compute features three ways; training/serving skew is degrading predictions.
scenarios.title: One definition of each feature
scenarios.why: SageMaker Feature Store centralizes feature definitions with online (low-latency serving) and offline (training) stores — one definition, no skew. Data Wrangler prepares data; S3 alone has no feature semantics; spreadsheets aren't infrastructure.

evidence: hpo.txt

Model sensitive to 8 hyperparameters.
Manual tuning: 3 weeks, still
underperforming.
scenarios.hint: Which SageMaker feature searches hyperparameters automatically?
scenarios.situation: A model sensitive to 8 hyperparameters; manual tuning took 3 weeks and still underperforms.
scenarios.title: Eight knobs, three weeks
scenarios.why: SageMaker automatic model tuning (hyperparameter optimization) searches the space systematically with strategies like Bayesian optimization — far more efficient than manual grids. Guessing and defaults leave performance on the table.

choices: Retraining on a fixed schedule only
evidence: drift.txt

Model in prod 8 months.
Accuracy decaying; input
distribution shifted.
scenarios.hint: Which service watches for data and prediction drift in production?
scenarios.situation: A production model's accuracy is decaying as input distribution shifts.
scenarios.title: The model that went stale
scenarios.why: SageMaker Model Monitor continuously watches endpoints for data drift, concept drift, and quality decay, alerting before damage compounds. Manual spot-checks miss gradual decay; fixed-schedule retraining may be too late or wasteful; no monitoring is blindness.

evidence: pipe2.txt

ML workflow: prepare -> train ->
evaluate -> register -> deploy.
Need: repeatable, auditable.
scenarios.hint: Which SageMaker service makes ML workflows into CI/CD pipelines?
scenarios.prompt: What makes the ML workflow repeatable?
scenarios.situation: A 5-stage ML workflow must be repeatable and auditable.
scenarios.title: CI/CD for machine learning
scenarios.why: SageMaker Pipelines defines ML workflows as code with steps, caching, and lineage — the MLOps equivalent of CI/CD. Giant notebooks aren't repeatable; bash scripts lack lineage; console clicks aren't auditable.

evidence: dist.txt

LLM fine-tune: 70B params.
Single GPU: OOM.
Need: finish this week.
scenarios.hint: 70B parameters can't fit one GPU — which SageMaker capability splits the work?
scenarios.situation: Fine-tuning a 70B-parameter model OOMs on a single GPU; it must finish this week.
scenarios.title: Seventy billion parameters, one week
scenarios.why: SageMaker distributed training (data and model parallelism libraries) shards the model and data across many GPUs, making 70B-parameter training feasible on a deadline. A single GPU can't hold it; CPU-only would take months; the compiler optimizes but doesn't shard.

choices: SageMaker Data Wrangler for visual prep + Processing jobs for production
No prep; hope the model copes
evidence: prep.txt

Raw data: missing values,
mixed formats, 50M rows.
Need: repeatable prep at scale.
scenarios.hint: Visual exploration plus scalable production jobs — which SageMaker combination?
scenarios.situation: 50M rows of messy data need repeatable preparation at scale.
scenarios.title: Fifty million messy rows
scenarios.why: Data Wrangler provides visual data preparation and exports the flow to SageMaker Processing jobs for repeatable production-scale execution. Raw-data training degrades models; Excel doesn't scale to 50M rows; hope isn't a strategy.

evidence: brew.txt

Analysts need to profile and clean
datasets visually, no code,
then operationalize.
scenarios.hint: Which no-code visual data-prep service integrates with Glue jobs?
scenarios.situation: Analysts need visual, no-code data profiling and cleaning that can be operationalized.
scenarios.title: Data prep without code
scenarios.why: Glue DataBrew provides visual no-code data preparation with profiling, and recipes convert to Glue jobs for production. Hand scripts per analyst don't scale; no profiling is blindness; production-only skips exploration.

choices: Stratified sampling / class weights / SMOTE-style resampling
evidence: imb.txt

Fraud labels: 0.1% positive.
Model predicts 'not fraud'
for everything: 99.9% accuracy.
scenarios.hint: 0.1% positives — what makes the model actually learn the minority class?
scenarios.prompt: What fixes the 'predict everything negative' model?
scenarios.situation: With 0.1% fraud labels, the model predicts 'not fraud' for everything and scores 99.9% accuracy.
scenarios.title: The model that learned nothing
scenarios.why: Imbalanced data needs stratified sampling, class weights, or resampling so the model actually learns the minority class — plus proper metrics (precision/recall/F1). Deleting the minority class removes the target; accuracy-only evaluation is what hid the failure.

choices: Dropping all rows with any missing value
Analysis-driven strategy: understand missingness, then impute or model appropriately
evidence: miss.txt

30% of income field missing.
Missingness correlates with
the target variable.
scenarios.hint: Missingness correlates with the target — what does that tell you about blind imputation?
scenarios.prompt: What handles the missing income field correctly?
scenarios.situation: 30% of the income field is missing, and the missingness correlates with the target.
scenarios.title: The missingness is the signal
scenarios.why: When missingness correlates with the target (MNAR), blind imputation or deletion biases the model; the correct approach analyzes the mechanism first, then chooses imputation/modeling that accounts for it (possibly including missingness indicators). Mean/zero imputation and wholesale deletion all distort.

choices: One-hot encoding for low-cardinality categories; embeddings/target encoding for high-cardinality
evidence: cat.txt

Features: 200 zip codes,
10 product categories,
5 regions.
scenarios.hint: Match the encoding to the cardinality — what's the standard pairing?
scenarios.situation: Features include 200 zip codes, 10 product categories, and 5 regions.
scenarios.title: Two hundred zip codes
scenarios.why: One-hot suits low-cardinality features (regions, categories); high-cardinality features like zip codes need embeddings or target encoding to avoid 200 sparse columns. Label encoding imposes false ordinality; ignoring loses signal; blind hashing loses interpretability.

choices: Feature scaling (standardization/normalization) for distance- and gradient-based models
evidence: scale2.txt

KNN model: income ($0-500k)
dominates age (0-100).
Predictions poor.
scenarios.hint: Distance-based models compare raw magnitudes — what equalizes the scales?
scenarios.prompt: What fixes the dominated distance metric?
scenarios.situation: A KNN model's distance metric is dominated by income ($0–500k) over age (0–100).
scenarios.title: When income drowns out age
scenarios.why: Feature scaling (standardization/normalization) puts features on comparable scales so distance- and gradient-based models treat them fairly. Unscaled training lets large-magnitude features dominate; scaling only the target doesn't fix feature distances.

choices: Training on the full dataset every time
Spot Instances for fault-tolerant training with checkpoints
evidence: cost3.txt

Training: 48h on 8 GPUs.
Budget tight. Job checkpoints
hourly; restarts are fine.
scenarios.hint: Checkpointed, restart-tolerant — which pricing cuts GPU cost deeply?
scenarios.situation: A 48-hour 8-GPU training job checkpoints hourly and tolerates restarts; budget is tight.
scenarios.title: Cheap GPUs that can be interrupted
scenarios.why: SageMaker Managed Spot Training uses Spot Instances for up to ~70% savings; hourly checkpoints make interruptions harmless. On-Demand wastes the discount; full retrains without checkpoints are fragile; laptops can't do this.

choices: SageMaker Experiments to track runs, metrics, and lineage
evidence: exp.txt

50 training runs.
Can't reproduce the best one.
Nobody knows which data
and code produced it.
scenarios.hint: Which SageMaker feature tracks the full lineage of every run?
scenarios.situation: 50 training runs; the best one can't be reproduced — data, code, and parameters are unknown.
scenarios.title: The run nobody can reproduce
scenarios.why: SageMaker Experiments tracks runs with parameters, metrics, data, and code lineage — making the best run reproducible. Spreadsheets drift; memory fades; no tracking guarantees irreproducibility.

evidence: overfit.txt

Validation loss decreasing then
rising; training loss still falling.
Compute budget limited.
scenarios.hint: Validation rising while training falls — what stops the waste?
scenarios.situation: Validation loss rises while training loss falls; the compute budget is limited.
scenarios.title: Stop when it stops learning
scenarios.why: Early stopping halts training when validation stops improving (saving compute and preventing overfitting), and learning-rate scheduling improves convergence. More epochs worsen overfitting; bigger models cost more without fixing it.

choices: Transfer learning: fine-tune a pre-trained model
evidence: transfer.txt

Task: classify support tickets.
Labeled data: 2,000 tickets.
Need: good accuracy, fast.
scenarios.hint: 2,000 labels isn't much — what leverages knowledge from larger datasets?
scenarios.prompt: What achieves good accuracy with 2,000 labels?
scenarios.situation: Support-ticket classification with only 2,000 labeled tickets needs good accuracy fast.
scenarios.title: Two thousand labels, big ambitions
scenarios.why: Transfer learning fine-tunes a pre-trained model, leveraging representations learned from massive data — effective with small labeled sets. Training from scratch on 2k labels underfits; rules engines don't generalize; random weights aren't a model.

choices: SageMaker Debugger / profiler to catch bad tensors and bottlenecks
evidence: debug.txt

Training loss: NaN at epoch 3.
No idea which layer or
which batch caused it.
scenarios.hint: Which SageMaker feature inspects tensors during training?
scenarios.situation: Training loss goes NaN at epoch 3; the failing layer and batch are unknown.
scenarios.title: Loss went NaN
scenarios.why: SageMaker Debugger inspects tensors during training with built-in rules that catch NaNs, vanishing gradients, and bottlenecks automatically. Print statements don't scale to tensor internals; guessing wastes runs.

evidence: prec.txt

Training too slow on budget GPUs.
Model supports AMP.
Need: 2x speed, same accuracy.
scenarios.hint: Which technique mixes FP16 and FP32 for speed without accuracy loss?
scenarios.situation: Training is too slow on budget GPUs; the model supports automatic mixed precision.
scenarios.title: Twice the speed, same accuracy
scenarios.why: Mixed-precision training (FP16 compute with FP32 master weights via AMP) roughly doubles throughput on modern GPUs with negligible accuracy impact. FP32-everywhere is the slow baseline; INT8 training from scratch risks accuracy; no GPUs is slower still.

evidence: rt.txt

API needs predictions in
<100ms, 24/7, spiky traffic.
scenarios.hint: Sub-100ms, always-on, spiky — which SageMaker inference option?
scenarios.situation: An API needs <100ms predictions 24/7 with spiky traffic.
scenarios.title: Predictions in under 100ms
scenarios.why: SageMaker real-time endpoints with auto-scaling serve low-latency predictions 24/7 and scale with spikes. Notebooks aren't production; batch transform is for offline; email isn't an API.

evidence: batch3.txt

Need: score 100M records
once a night. No latency
requirement.
scenarios.hint: 100M records, no latency SLA — which option is cheapest?
scenarios.situation: 100M records need scoring once nightly with no latency requirement.
scenarios.title: One hundred million, overnight
scenarios.why: Batch Transform is the cost-effective choice for large offline inference — no always-on endpoint needed. Real-time endpoints idle between batches; Lambda has payload/time limits unsuited to 100M records.

evidence: ab.txt

New model version.
Need: 5% live traffic, compare
metrics, instant rollback.
scenarios.hint: Which endpoint feature splits traffic between variants?
scenarios.prompt: What validates the new version safely?
scenarios.situation: A new model version needs 5% live traffic with metric comparison and instant rollback.
scenarios.title: Five percent of traffic, zero regret
scenarios.why: Endpoint production variants enable canary and A/B (shadow) testing with traffic splitting and instant rollback. All-at-once updates risk 100% of traffic; manual swaps are slow; separate accounts don't split traffic.

evidence: edge.txt

Need: run vision model on
warehouse cameras (limited
compute, intermittent network).
scenarios.hint: Limited compute, intermittent network — what shrinks the model for the edge?
scenarios.situation: A vision model must run on warehouse cameras with limited compute and intermittent connectivity.
scenarios.title: AI on a camera
scenarios.why: Model optimization (quantization, distillation, pruning via SageMaker Neo/Edge) shrinks models for edge devices, and edge deployment runs offline. Full-size models don't fit; no optimization fails the constraints; bigger models worsen them.

evidence: reg.txt

12 model versions in prod
history. Audit asks: which version
is live, approved by whom?
scenarios.hint: Which SageMaker feature versions models with approval workflows?
scenarios.situation: Twelve model versions exist; the audit needs to know which is live and who approved it.
scenarios.title: Which model is live?
scenarios.why: The SageMaker Model Registry versions models with metadata, approval workflows, and deployment tracking — the auditable answer. Shared drives and email lack versioning and approvals; no registry is unauditable.

choices: Closed-loop MLOps: monitor -> trigger retraining -> validate -> deploy via pipelines
evidence: loop.txt

Data drifts seasonally.
Need: detect drift, retrain,
validate, redeploy — automatically.
scenarios.hint: Which pattern closes the loop from monitoring to redeployment?
scenarios.situation: Seasonal data drift requires automatic detect-retrain-validate-redeploy.
scenarios.title: Closing the loop
scenarios.why: Closed-loop MLOps (Model Monitor → retraining trigger → Pipelines validation → deployment) automates the full cycle. Blind scheduled retraining wastes compute and may deploy worse models; never/manual retraining lets drift compound.

choices: Amazon Bedrock: managed foundation models via API
evidence: bedrock.txt

Need: summarization + Q&A over
docs. No ML team. Data must
stay private. Budget: moderate.
scenarios.hint: Which service offers foundation models as a managed API?
scenarios.situation: Document summarization and Q&A needed with no ML team; data must stay private.
scenarios.title: GenAI without an ML team
scenarios.why: Bedrock provides managed foundation models via API — no training infrastructure, with data-privacy commitments (inputs not used for training). Training from scratch needs an ML team and massive budget; laptops can't do it.

choices: RAG: retrieve relevant chunks, then generate with Bedrock
Bigger prompts with the whole corpus
evidence: rag.txt

Q&A over 10k internal docs.
Model hallucinates internal facts.
Docs update weekly.
scenarios.hint: Hallucinations + changing docs — what grounds the model in your data?
scenarios.prompt: What grounds answers in the actual documents?
scenarios.situation: Q&A over 10k internal docs; the model hallucinates internal facts and docs update weekly.
scenarios.title: Stop the hallucinations
scenarios.why: Retrieval-Augmented Generation retrieves relevant chunks (e.g., via Knowledge Bases for Bedrock with OpenSearch/vector store) and grounds generation in them — handling weekly updates without retraining. Fine-tuning weekly is expensive; whole-corpus prompts don't fit context windows; hope isn't engineering.

choices: Bedrock fine-tuning / continued pre-training for smaller adaptations; prompt engineering first
evidence: ft.txt

Need: model speaks in the
company's support tone.
Budget: small. Data: 500 examples.
scenarios.hint: Small budget, 500 examples, tone adaptation — what's the lightest effective customization?
scenarios.situation: The model must adopt the company's support tone; budget is small with 500 examples.
scenarios.title: Teaching the model your tone
scenarios.why: Prompt engineering first, then Bedrock fine-tuning for the tone adaptation — the lightest effective path for 500 examples on a small budget. Full 70B fine-tuning is overkill; training from scratch is infeasible; no customization misses the requirement.

choices: Bedrock Guardrails: content filters, PII redaction, denied topics
evidence: guard2.txt

Customer-facing chatbot.
Requirement: block harmful content,
redact PII, refuse off-topic
requests.
scenarios.hint: Which Bedrock feature enforces content policies?
scenarios.situation: A customer-facing chatbot must block harmful content, redact PII, and refuse off-topic requests.
scenarios.title: Guardrails for the chatbot
scenarios.why: Bedrock Guardrails enforce content filters, PII redaction, and denied topics consistently at the API layer. Trusting the model is the current risk; manual review of every output doesn't scale; no guardrails fails the requirement.

choices: Amazon Bedrock Agents / agentic workflows with tool use
evidence: agent.txt

Task: book travel = search flights,
check calendar, confirm, notify.
Multi-step with tools.
scenarios.hint: Multi-step tasks with tool calls — which pattern orchestrates them?
scenarios.situation: Booking travel requires searching flights, checking calendars, confirming, and notifying — multi-step with tools.
scenarios.title: The agent that books travel
scenarios.why: Bedrock Agents (agentic workflows) let foundation models plan multi-step tasks and call tools/APIs — the pattern for this use case. Longer prompts don't add tool use; a bigger model alone doesn't orchestrate; fine-tuning doesn't create agency.

evidence: jump.txt

Need: evaluate 5 open models
quickly for a classification task.
Team: 2 engineers.
scenarios.hint: Which SageMaker feature offers pre-trained models deployable in clicks?
scenarios.prompt: What lets the small team evaluate models fast?
scenarios.situation: Two engineers need to evaluate 5 open models quickly for a classification task.
scenarios.title: Five models, one afternoon
scenarios.why: SageMaker JumpStart provides pre-trained and foundation models deployable/evaluable quickly — ideal for small-team evaluation. Training from scratch wastes the evaluation goal; laptops can't serve these models; manual infra slows everything.
